$ rg "[^-]readability-function-size" --hidden -l

phosphor-psu-code-mgmt/.clang-tidy
phosphor-led-manager/.clang-tidy

`readability-function-size` are even enabled by bmcweb, entity-manager, and dbus-sensors.  So it at least seems like that one isn't an issue?

https://clang.llvm.org/extra/clang-tidy/checks/readability/function-size.html

The default value is `none` which is no-op, right?

So the check is enabled without any effect.

There is a `StatementThreshold` which seems to default to 800.
Done

> or we'd have to raise the limits to
where they were not useful.

IMO the *correct interpretation* of the line count check would be to simply have a limit which matches the current largest function.

Then anyone interested can break down that function and lower the value.

At some point then we can arrive at the recommended value.

Understand this is a *monotonic process* and not something to be done in a single patch.

> While I'm hopeful that these checks could
be enabled in the future,

With this change you are actively working against such a future by removing the check from the list.


Extra note:

Not sure if a clang-format upgrade could cause problems with line count check.
In which case, we could simply increase the line count check by a small amount.

> With this change you are actively working against such a future by removing the check from the list.

For all the repos I've enabled tidy on, the lack of a reference wasn't what stopped enabling these, it was actual engineering and social problems.  IF we find a way to enable these, and someone is signed up to figure out the technical problems with them, I'm in support, but this reference has been present for almost 2 years, and we haven't made progress.  I'd rather documentation handle the bulk of our repositories and be generally useful, as the commit message states.

> I'm in support, but this reference has been present for almost 2 years, and we haven't made progress.

We did make progress on this. I sometimes reference cpp core guidelines for function size and having these statements in our documented `.clang-tidy` file here helps to remove any ambiguity about where the project wants to go.


>  IF we find a way to enable these, and someone is signed up to figure out the technical problems with them, I'm in support,

You do not have to go to 60 lines right away. You can start with some realistic goal for the repos you maintain, and `NOLINT` the functions which are too big.

Then at least you do not get any new functions exceeding that size, and people can work on the problematic ones on their own time.


I do not see any technical problems. If you refer to inline lambda size, it is an interpretation issue. If you want an option to count inline lambdas towards the size, that's something to contribute to the clang-tidy project.

To reinforce my point here, created this change for EM
https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/entity-manager/+/82811

We can set the line threshold to 170 in EM repo now, which is only around triple what cpp core guidelines recommends.

Pending refactor of a few bloated functions we could probably go to 120 in a few months or so if anyone is interested.

It also helps in the review since the context one needs to look at for reviewing a change gets smaller.

> documented .clang-tidy file here helps to remove any ambiguity about where the project wants to go.

Can we just document that outside of the actual file?  Putting these checks in the .clang-tidy file means we can't deploy them across the repos without maintainers doing work.  I get wanting some documentation, I'd kind of assume cpp core guidelines does a good job of that, and we just need to amend some other recommendations for limits?  IMO, if we have limits they should be written down in prose rather than having to dig up a config file.

> We can set the line threshold to 170 in EM repo now,

As the EM maintainer, I'm happy to have that conversation in the EM review, but that still doesn't allow us to enable this check in EM as it's defined here, so I'm not sure how it helps.  I'm VERY happy to see some amount of progress on this, but I don't think that review alone changes the need for this commit.  Most of the checks in the next commit have been enabled for years.

> NOLINT the functions which are too big.

I think I mentioned this in one of the other comments, but this meant that far too many functions needed NOLINT, and it became a maintenance problem.

> Putting these checks in the .clang-tidy file means we can't deploy them across the repos without maintainers doing work.

You can not just 'deploy' most of these checks. People have to do the work to enable them.

Which is also true for the reference checks you are planning to add here.

>  IMO, if we have limits they should be written down in prose rather than having to dig up a config file.

If you want something to just 'roll out' without doing any work, then set the limit to 9000 or something and leave in the comment about cpp core guidelines and their recommended value.

> > Putting these checks in the .clang-tidy file means we can't deploy them across the repos without maintainers doing work.
> 
> You can not just 'deploy' most of these checks. People have to do the work to enable them.
> 
> Which is also true for the reference checks you are planning to add here.

That hasn't been my experience.  The majority of these checks can be applied without a ton of maintainer effort.  The first tidy file in 2020 was added in a day or two.  Many of the checks have "fix" capabilities, that will just fix the code for you.  Put that in a PR, and you're done.

> 
> >  IMO, if we have limits they should be written down in prose rather than having to dig up a config file.
> 
> If you want something to just 'roll out' without doing any work, then set the limit to 9000 or something and leave in the comment about cpp core guidelines and their recommended value.

There is no value in a check that has a limit of 9000, and just adds to our runtime.  I am happy to document it in another file.
Done

I had a similar experience running into issues when I tried enabling this on PLDM, and encountered similar challenges while working with SPDM as well. In addition , the terminology used in the PLDM and SPDM specifications can sometimes be quite extensive, which makes it difficult to translate directly into code. If we simplify or alter the terms/symbol names just to pass length checks, it can become challenging to maintain a clear mapping to the original specifications.

If that's a regular thing (not just a few functions), then why not just enable some of these checks, with somewhat higher values?

For example if you regularly find yourself writing 200 line functions which are conceptually simple and easy to understand despite the length, maybe that is a good starting point for your repos?
I think we got that question answered in the other thread.  Closing this out, please reopen if there are other concerns.

> As a side note, one thing asio-based repos suffer from is overly large inline lambdas. cognative comlexity and length checks do not take those
into account when measuring line count, and in some cases seem to
actively disable the checks, so even if we were able to enable these
checks, as implemented in clang they're not useful in a lot of scenarios
today.

Your argument goes like "The check for problem A is not useful because it does not work right in presence of problem B. So we can remove the check for problem A".

Then just remove problem B. It needs to be removed anyways.

For the rest of the functions without inline lambdas, it works right, so it has value there.

From a compiler perspective, inline lembdas could be seen as separate functions. So maybe the tooling does work right with that interpretation.

> Then just remove problem B. It needs to be removed anyways.

Sure, lets remove problem B (you and I have both been working on it), but if we had to enable this check and enforce it, it would take effort away from cleaning up B to work on A which is less important.  It is about noting that even IF we were able to enable this check, there are technical limitations in tidy that prevent it being useful in many real contexts.  If you're suggesting I go fix tidy, I've thought about it, but that doesn't change anything about this path.

> but if we had to enable this check and enforce it, it would take effort away from cleaning up B to work on A which is less important.

It's documented that it does not have to be enforced yet, and certainly not at 60 lines per function.

We can discuss about a realistic line count or parameter count, but there has to be a limit somewhere, and ideally it should be documented.

> > but if we had to enable this check and enforce it, it would take effort away from cleaning up B to work on A which is less important.
> 
> It's documented that it does not have to be enforced yet, and certainly not at 60 lines per function.

Right..... but that's preventing people from using this file.  The next patchset turns this into a "reference" of checks that we've enabled and know can work on our codebases.

> 
> We can discuss about a realistic line count or parameter count, but there has to be a limit somewhere, and ideally it should be documented.

cpp core guidelines warns against enforcement, but does document some recommendations for length and arg count, so I think we have that even after this patch.

> Right..... but that's preventing people from using this file. The next patchset turns this into a "reference" of checks that we've enabled and know can work on our codebases.

It works on the 2 codebases you got the list from. Not sure if it will work on any other repos?

> cpp core guidelines warns against enforcement, but does document some recommendations for length and arg count, so I think we have that even after this patch.

I am fine if we drop the checks for complexity and parameter count for now.

But the function line count is something i want to stay in here.

> > Right..... but that's preventing people from using this file. The next patchset turns this into a "reference" of checks that we've enabled and know can work on our codebases.
> 
> It works on the 2 codebases you got the list from. Not sure if it will work on any other repos?

No, I don't know that for a fact, but I would suspect it would.  There are more repositories that have enabled these checks other than the two I mentioned, enough that I believe that the average maintainer can enable these.  With that said, if as we go along, we find specific checks that are too onerous, this list is changable.

> 
> > cpp core guidelines warns against enforcement, but does document some recommendations for length and arg count, so I think we have that even after this patch.
> 
> I am fine if we drop the checks for complexity and parameter count for now.
> 
> But the function line count is something i want to stay in here.

Can I document it outside this file somewhere (maybe clang-tidy-next.md)?  I know you mentioned increasing the value to 9000 lines, but I'd rather we document intent with the real number.  Something like "There is general agreement that we would LIKE code to be able to conform to these checks, but are attempting to roll out changes across the repos, so these checks cannot be enabled yet."

I am fine with this approach if you need something to roll out without too much effort. That way we avoid pulling any value like `9000` or `200` out of thin air.

Would prefer something like `.clang-tidy-next` so people can just copy-past from one to the other. Ideally right next to the `.clang-tidy` file.

Suggested contents:

```
# This file contains additional checks we would like to enable in the future.

Checks: '-*,
    readability-function-size,
    '
CheckOptions:
-   key: readability-function-size.LineThreshold
    value: 60 # [1]
-   key: readability-function-size.ParameterThreshold
    value: 6  # [2]

# [1] https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines#f3-keep-functions-short-and-simple
# [2] https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines#f2-a-function-should-perform-a-single-logical-operation

```
👍. Have broken this out into its own file.

There is absolutely no requirement for any 'experience' what-so-ever.

We can simply take what's been written down in those core guidelines, which have been documented by people who are actually C++ experts.

The OpenBMC project has already documented it is trying to follow these guidelines.

https://github.com/openbmc/docs/blob/ac6e69a7df9c214fbf55144aafde43595a76aa60/cpp-style-and-conventions.md?plain=1#L73

> We can simply take what's been written down in those core guidelines

I do agree with the overall intent of the Core Guidelines w.r.t. function length and function behavior.  But, the Core Guidelines are also vague as to what the "enforcement" would be of long line length.  The core guidelines do not talk about "cognative" or cyclomatic complexity.  I don't think it is really sufficient to point to the words in the Core Guidelines as the rationale for these.

> There is absolutely no requirement for any 'experience' what-so-ever.

No, not necessarily, but negative experience is certainly a reason for removing this, which is the data Ed is bringing.

> negative experience is certainly a reason for removing this

negative experience in terms of "we could not bring the function size down to 60 lines"
IMO shows that the project overall is not ready to try and enforce this value.

Maybe we need to come up with a project-specific value which is a more realistic value. Something like 200.

Then in the future if the goal has been reached then the goalpost can be moved.

I guess we did not do that the first time around since people were asking for concrete sources and not arbitrary values (if i remember correctly).

> IMO shows that the project overall is not ready to try and enforce this value.

This is exactly what I'm trying to say in this patch.

> I don't think it is really sufficient to point to the words in the Core Guidelines as the rationale for these.

I had similar thoughts around cppcoreguildelines enforcement recommendations, but I didn't articulate it in the commit message.


> Maybe we need to come up with a project-specific value which is a more realistic value. Something like 200.

I've tried exactly this (I think I picked 250) and the number of functions that needed to change was still too high, and because of the lambda problem, didn't even target the most complex code we had that should be the highest priority to clean up.  If I'm personally going to spend time cleaning things up, it will be the deeply nested lambda garbage that we have a lot of experience to know causes problems (and I greatly appreciate your patches you send to help clean up).  Enabling this check doesn't align with those goals, and actively distracts from cleanup of the worst code we have.

> I've tried exactly this (I think I picked 250) and the number of functions that needed to change was still too high, and because of the lambda problem, didn't even target the most complex code we had that should be the highest priority to clean up

Then go to 350 or something. Better to have some limit there than no limit at all.

I agree that cleaning up inline lambdas is more important. So if by extracting an inline lambda you exceed the line count, simply NOLINT the function and come back to it at a later time.
It's not a heavy lift.


> enabling this check doesn't align with those goals, and actively distracts from cleanup of the worst code we have.

How does it distract? You have your own priorities for cleanup. No one is forcing you to prioritize this issue.
Done
